method_note: Team-by-team, manually reviewed fantasy implications from all 32 authenticated coaching breakdowns. Summaries are paraphrased, uncertainty is retained, and broad or unresolved claims remain research-only. Small reviewed adjustments are capped and expire so this one expert source cannot dominate consensus rankings.

coverage.limitation: This track captures the coaching-guide analysis. Current injuries, depth charts, and structured models are refreshed separately.

signals.summary: Buffalo remains a run-led, play-action offense with Josh Allen controlling checks and a stronger receiving group around him.
signals.mechanism: Continuity, a productive line, and clearer high-value roles support the primary Bills skill players, while complex option rules can punish receivers who do not earn Allen's trust.

signals.summary: Miami's rebuilt staff still plans to center the offense on De'Von Achane in both the run and short passing games.
signals.mechanism: Wide-zone volume and a large receiving role provide multiple paths to production even if game script or the passing personnel disappoints.

signals.summary: New England's motion, RPO, and play-action structure gives Drake Maye clearer reads and now pairs him with a deeper receiving group.
signals.mechanism: Improved weapons and designed rushing can raise the quarterback ceiling, though Maye's tendency to distribute targets limits confidence in any one secondary receiver.

signals.summary: The Jets have publicly discussed splitting backfield touches among three runners despite Breece Hall being the most dangerous option.
signals.mechanism: A real three-way rotation would reduce Hall's snap and touch ceiling, but the coaching plan is not yet proven in regular-season usage.

signals.summary: Baltimore is installing a new run-first spread system with play action, creating upside but also a meaningful early-season learning curve.
signals.mechanism: The design fits Lamar Jackson, Derrick Henry, and Zay Flowers, while a completely new staff and playbook make the timing and magnitude uncertain.

signals.summary: Cincinnati retains a concentrated, quick-game passing attack built around Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, and defined red-zone roles.
signals.mechanism: Continuity and concentrated opportunity make the core Bengals options comparatively dependable even though the offense plays slower than its reputation suggests.

signals.summary: Cleveland enters a rebuild with an unsettled multi-quarterback plan and a new staff that may struggle to establish a stable passing hierarchy.
signals.mechanism: Quarterback changes can disrupt timing, target quality, and weekly receiver roles, creating unusually high redraft volatility.

signals.summary: Mike McCarthy's offense projects Jaylen Warren for passing-down work while Rico Dowdle handles more early-down and goal-line snaps.
signals.mechanism: Aaron Rodgers' recent tendency to target running backs gives Warren a useful receiving path, though the split limits the ceiling of both backs.

signals.summary: Houston's offense remains conservative and matchup-driven despite having receivers capable of winning downfield.
signals.mechanism: If the staff continues to prioritize avoiding mistakes over aggression, C.J. Stroud and the vertical receivers may have less passing volume and ceiling than their talent implies.

signals.summary: Houston projects David Montgomery for lead and red-zone work, with Woody Marks serving more as a change-of-pace receiver.
signals.mechanism: Early-down and goal-line volume is particularly useful in non-PPR scoring and can sustain value without a dominant receiving share.

signals.summary: Indianapolis lost a starting tackle and its boundary target while relying on Daniel Jones after several major injuries.
signals.mechanism: Weaker protection, less formation-defining receiver gravity, and quarterback durability uncertainty lower the stability of the offense around Jonathan Taylor and the wideouts.

signals.summary: Jacksonville's staff sees Bhayshul Tuten in the lead role, with Chris Rodriguez carrying direct contingency and red-zone value.
signals.mechanism: A productive scheme and defined handcuff path create upside, but Tuten's ball security remains a role risk.

signals.summary: Tennessee replaced its staff with Robert Saleh, Brian Daboll, and a new line coach, installing a run-first offense built on horizontal spacing, quick throws, RPOs, and play action.
signals.mechanism: The design could make reads easier for Cam Ward and create clearer receiver roles, but the entire projection depends on Ward's development and the line executing a changed blocking mix.

signals.summary: Brian Daboll's spacing, pre-snap motion, RPO, and play-action concepts are designed to simplify Cam Ward's reads after a stronger finish to his rookie season.
signals.mechanism: Higher-percentage answers and a coach with a history of quarterback development create breakout potential, while Ward's own execution remains the central uncertainty.

signals.summary: Wan'Dale Robinson is a direct fit for Daboll's quick underneath routes and already succeeded in a similar role under him.
signals.mechanism: Screens, drags, and crossing routes align with Robinson's short-area strengths and offer a credible path to stable target volume.

signals.summary: Carnell Tate is projected to begin as Tennessee's primary vertical threat in a play-action offense.
signals.mechanism: A defined deep role creates non-PPR splash-play upside, but rookie development and Cam Ward's deep execution make the weekly floor uncertain.

signals.summary: Tennessee's run-first plan can support Tony Pollard if the new line coach emphasizes the zone concepts that best fit him.
signals.mechanism: Pollard's value rises with successful zone blocking, but poor interior movement or a shift toward man-gap concepts could redirect work to Nicholas Singleton.

signals.summary: Nicholas Singleton could earn a larger Tennessee role if the rebuilt line leans toward the man-gap concepts that fit him better than Tony Pollard.
signals.mechanism: The blocking mix creates a conditional path to a significant niche rather than a verified current workload.

signals.summary: Sean Payton's offense remains productive but unusually difficult to project outside quarterback because weekly personnel usage changes frequently.
signals.mechanism: The scheme can create efficient touches, but volatile snap and touch allocation lowers confidence in secondary Denver skill players.

signals.summary: Kansas City rebuilt around a stronger run game and expects to lean on it while Patrick Mahomes completes his return from an ACL injury.
signals.mechanism: Early rushing volume and Kenneth Walker's all-purpose fit raise the value of the backfield, though the balance may change as Mahomes regains full confidence.

signals.summary: Mike McDaniel joins Jim Harbaugh with added blockers and a plan centered on Omarion Hampton while reducing the need for Justin Herbert to run.
signals.mechanism: The line and run design strongly support Hampton; better protection helps Herbert, but fewer designed scrambles can offset some quarterback upside.

signals.summary: Klint Kubiak and Rick Dennison bring a proven system that is expected to feature Ashton Jeanty and use Brock Bowers as the primary movable mismatch.
signals.mechanism: Concentrated roles in a run-led, play-action structure support both cornerstone players even if wide receiver volume stays limited.

signals.summary: Dallas retains a fast, pass-heavy offense with two dangerous receivers and an improved, scheme-versatile line supporting a high-snap lead back.
signals.mechanism: Pace and concentrated high-value roles support CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Javonte Williams even if raw rushing volume is modest.

signals.summary: New York's new staff upgraded the line and plans a high-volume RPO run game with Isaiah Likely in a prominent quick-read role.
signals.mechanism: Better protection and defined RPO answers support Jaxson Dart and Likely, although the offense still must prove the transition works in games.

signals.summary: Philadelphia's new passing identity is expected to attack intermediate areas more often after A.J. Brown's departure, concentrating opportunity around DeVonta Smith.
signals.mechanism: A clearer lead role and route emphasis that fits Smith can raise both target share and weekly consistency.

signals.summary: Washington handed its offense to first-time coordinator David Blough, with broad player freedom but little evidence yet that the many concepts will form a coherent system.
signals.mechanism: The talent and tempo create upside, while play-calling inexperience and uncertain role integration raise execution risk.

signals.summary: Chicago returns Ben Johnson's versatile run-first offense with improved line depth and defined short-area and vertical roles.
signals.mechanism: The structure creates easier throws for Caleb Williams while preserving deep-shot upside and a productive rushing base.

signals.summary: Detroit's new coordinator is expected to feature Jahmyr Gibbs and use a rhythm passing game that emphasizes Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta over the middle.
signals.mechanism: Concentrated touches and a coordinator history favorable to tight ends support the primary Lions options, though Jared Goff must adapt to added control at the line.

signals.summary: Green Bay reduced its receiver rotation but still projects Christian Watson and Jayden Reed into different specialized roles rather than one dominant target funnel.
signals.mechanism: Fewer bodies help, yet role specialization can keep weekly volume uneven and makes the hierarchy important to monitor.

signals.summary: Minnesota's offense remains pass-led and concentrated around Justin Jefferson, with short play-action concepts also supporting T.J. Hockenson.
signals.mechanism: The target funnel protects the primary pass catchers from some of the uncertainty created by a possible multi-quarterback season.

signals.summary: Kevin Stefanski and elite line coach Bill Callahan bring a wide-zone plan expected to run through Bijan Robinson, with Kyle Pitts positioned for short-area work.
signals.mechanism: A stabilized line and scheme fit support high rushing efficiency and receiving access for the offense's two most important mismatch players.

signals.summary: Carolina's slow, quick-pass offense supports its running backs and shallow-route receivers but remains vulnerable when defenses vary pressure against simple protection rules.
signals.mechanism: High-percentage throws and run volume create usable roles, while the protection design and Bryce Young's limited ceiling constrain explosive output.

signals.summary: New Orleans upgraded its weak line spot and added explosive runners and receivers to a flexible Kellen Moore offense.
signals.mechanism: Better protection and more explosive personnel open space for Travis Etienne and Chris Olave, though the ceiling still depends on Tyler Shough taking a second-year step.

signals.summary: Tampa Bay's new offense emphasizes quick yards-after-catch throws and more running-back targets, with Emeka Egbuka moved around the formation.
signals.mechanism: The design fits versatile backs and Egbuka, but it is a less natural fit for Baker Mayfield's preferred approach.

signals.summary: FantasyGuru questions Baker Mayfield's fit in Zac Robinson's shotgun- and pistol-heavy offense.
signals.mechanism: A scheme mismatch can reduce efficiency and timing even if Mayfield's competitiveness preserves volume and job security.

signals.summary: Arizona improved its line and installed Mike LaFleur's system, but expected quarterback regression could cap the passing-game volume available to its receivers.
signals.mechanism: Better design cannot fully offset weaker quarterback efficiency, reducing confidence in repeat target totals for the top pass catchers.

signals.summary: The Rams retain Sean McVay's concentrated, proven offense with tight formations supporting quick receivers and Kyren Williams holding the high-value backfield work.
signals.mechanism: Continuity and clearly assigned passing-down, goal-line, and primary receiving roles improve projection stability for the core players.

signals.summary: San Francisco continues to evolve its short, run-led offense and added personnel that may reopen more deep opportunities for Brock Purdy.
signals.mechanism: Kyle Shanahan's interchangeable formations sustain efficiency while the new vertical threats add ceiling without replacing the established underneath roles.

signals.summary: Seattle lost the coaches who drove its title offense and now relies on a first-time play caller while replacing its lead runner without a clear second receiver.
signals.mechanism: Similar early concepts may mask the transition, but weaker week-to-week adjustment, rushing efficiency, and target support create regression risk.
